name: Signal Watch — the lanterns answer each other
observation:
The five distant towers already in spire.js (merged `towers` mesh + the single merged `windows` quad mesh at ~62m) stop being static night-lights and start signalling. A 21-second cycle is divided into five 4.0s SLOTS plus a 1.0s all-quiet rest, and the slots run in clockwise bearing order, so the "speaking" light sweeps steadily round the horizon once per cycle and the player turns their body to follow it — a lookout's rhythm, not a maths test.

Inside a slot exactly two things happen, and they look nothing alike:
- SPEAKS: the slot's own lantern blinks hard and fast above its resting glow — N sharp blinks, 0.30s on / 0.30s off, starting at slot+0.20s, N in 1..4 (so it ends by slot+2.60s).
- ANSWERS: after a 0.30s pause, ONE OTHER lantern somewhere on the horizon comes up to a long, steady, un-blinking hold from slot+2.90s to slot+3.90s, then falls back to its resting glow.

Every lantern keeps its dim resting glow at all other times, so the skyline still reads as five inhabited windows (the room's existing character, and what a waiting finisher stares at) — the puzzle is entirely in the brightness envelope, not in windows switching off.

Two facts the player can get by watching, each without the other:
1. WHO ANSWERS WHOM, seen directly, whenever the speaker and the answerer happen to be in the same view (bearings are 30-90 degrees apart, so several pairs fit one screen).
2. HOW MANY BLINKS each lantern speaks, readable one lantern at a time from anywhere.

And the bearing of any lantern is read off the floor azimuth rose that is already baked into `makeFloorTexture()` — stand on the rose, face the lantern, sight out along the gold spoke running under your feet, and read the three-digit numeral it points to. Towers are re-placed onto exact 30-degree marks so the numeral is exact, never estimated.
deduction:
The "oh, THAT's what's happening" is two clicks, half a minute apart.

CLICK ONE (visual): the towers are not blinking decoratively, they are TALKING. A lantern blinks, and a different lantern answers with one long steady hold. Nobody had to tell you; you catch a speaker and its answerer in the same frame and it is obvious. Now you want to know who answers whom for all five — and you can't, because the five span up to 180 degrees of sky and you cannot watch both ends of the horizon at once. Half the pairs happen behind your back.

CLICK TWO (the real deduction): THE NUMBER OF BLINKS IS THE DISTANCE TO THE ANSWERER. Not a name, not a bearing — a count of lanterns, clockwise, from the speaker. A lantern that blinks 3 is answered by the third lantern clockwise round from it. The player verifies this against a pair they DID see with their own eyes ("the 180 one blinked three times and the 120 one answered — 240, 270, 120, yes, three round"), and from then on they can resolve every pair they could never see, including the ones behind them, from the blink counts alone.

Assemble it and the five arrows close into ONE unbroken loop that visits all five lanterns and comes back — the generator guarantees a single 5-cycle, so every lantern has exactly one caller and exactly one lantern it calls. That closed loop is the deduction. It is a shape the player draws on paper, not a value they read.

What the player CANNOT do is know where on that loop to cut it. The loop has no beginning, and no lantern on it is distinguished by anything visible in the sky. That is the gap the neighbour fills.

Design notes that make the deduction honest:
- The blink-count rule is discoverable, not stated: the Fragment says "count the blinks — they are not decoration" and nothing more.
- Two independent routes to the same map (watch the answer / decode the count) means an unlucky player who mis-sees one pair is corrected by the other route rather than silently wrong.
- Counts are deliberately irregular per session; a chain built on a constant hop (all counts equal) is rejected by the generator, because a uniform count teaches nothing and lets a player skip the rule.
answerFormat: 6 digits — two three-digit compass bearings run together, caller first, callee second, e.g. "240150" (spoken "two four zero, one five zero"). Digits only, so nothing collides read aloud; all bearings drawn from 120-300 so none has a leading zero and there is no 090-vs-90 ambiguity. `answersMatch()` already strips spaces and hyphens, so "240-150" also passes.
neighbourKeyRole:
The neighbour holds RELAY LANTERN — one lantern named by colour and chamber, e.g. `value: "BLUE — VAULT"`. That is the cut point on the loop, and nothing else.

It is emphatically not the answer: the key names a lantern, the answer is the two OTHER lanterns adjacent to it in a chain the Spire player had to build by watching the sky for two minutes. Someone handed the key with no observation has nothing — they don't know which window is blue, what its bearing is, or who flanks it. Someone with the full chain and no key has five equally plausible answers and a 30s lockout per wrong guess (`LOCKOUT_MS`), so a five-way brute force costs about two minutes of the run and reads to the crew as exactly what it is.

It also gates ORDER as well as selection: "the one that calls it, then the one it calls" is directionally meaningful only once you know which lantern is the pivot, and the loop is directional (reversing it gives a different, wrong pair).

The thematic payoff is the point of the whole chamber: the Spire is the only room that can see the others, and the key is literally your neighbour saying "that light out there is mine." You then tell the crew who is talking TO them and who they are talking to. If the key names the gold lantern the Spire player is looking at their own window — allowed, and worth the moment.

Suggested wording so it survives a voice call: label "RELAY LANTERN", value "BLUE — VAULT". Colour first, because "the blue one" is what actually gets said; chamber second, so a crew that has not memorised the palette still gets there.
seededValues: The five tower bearings: 5 chosen from the 30-degree marks [120,150,180,210,240,270,300], required to span at least 120 degrees and to include at least one adjacent 30-degree pair so some caller/answerer pairs are co-visible in one view. Replaces the hardcoded TOWER_BEARINGS = [62,108,156,212,268].

The hue-to-tower assignment: which chamber colour (vellum/Archive, lime/Engine, violet/Observatory, blue/Vault, gold/Spire) sits on which bearing — a seeded shuffle of windowAtlas.cells across the five quads, so 'the blue one' is never the same direction twice (120 possibilities).

The relay chain: a uniformly random single 5-cycle over the five lanterns (24 distinct cycles), from which the blink counts are derived as clockwise hop distances in 1..4. Rejected and re-rolled if all five counts are equal.
Which lantern the key names (5 possibilities) — this alone selects one of five distinct valid answers from the same chain.
Tower widths and heights already come from lcg(7717); move them onto the session seed too so the skyline silhouette differs per run at zero cost.

geometryChanges.change: Per-lantern brightness on the EXISTING merged window mesh: add a `color` BufferAttribute (20 vertices, 60 floats) to the geometry from makeAtlasQuads(), set windowMaterial.vertexColors = true, and write five brightness values into it each frame from a pure signalBrightness(lanternIndex, t, seed). Keeps the five windows in one mesh and one AdditiveBlending draw call; splitting them into five meshes is the trap and would blow the budget.
geometryChanges.cost: 0 new draw calls, 0 new lights. 60-float attribute upload per frame.

geometryChanges.change: Re-tint makeWindowAtlas(): the current inner core is rgba(255,250,235,0.92) near-white in every cell, so all five windows read as the same white dot at 62m and 'the blue one' is unfindable. Mix the core 60/40 toward the cell's hue, keep only a small white centre, and raise the window quad from 3.4 to 4.2m so the hue survives the dawn wash.
geometryChanges.cost: Texture-only; same 256x64 atlas, same quads. 0 draw calls.

geometryChanges.change: Sighting spokes on the floor rose in makeFloorTexture(): twelve faint gold radial lines (rgba(255,210,122,0.25), 2px) from the inner ring r=0.06 out to r=0.40 at every 30 degrees, so a player can lay a spoke under their feet and follow it out to a lantern instead of eyeballing an azimuth. This is what turns the rose from decoration into the instrument the puzzle uses.
geometryChanges.cost: Texture-only, one extra draw loop at bake time. 0 draw calls.

geometryChanges.change: Seeded tower placement: createSpire({ dimensions, seed, epoch }); TOWER_BEARINGS and the hue order come from lcg(seed) instead of the hardcoded arrays. scenes.js forwards prompt.seed / prompt.epoch through createRoom(id, options), which already passes options to the factory.

Dawn must stop erasing the signal: applyDawn() currently drives windowMaterial.opacity down to 0.35 at full light, which at DAWN_SECONDS=100 means the puzzle dims out roughly a minute after arrival. Floor it at 0.60 and let the vertex-colour brightness (resting 0.45, blink 1.0, hold 0.85) do the modulation on top.

Signal phase anchored to the run, not the mount: use t = (Date.now() - epoch)/1000 for the cycle phase (falling back to `elapsed` if epoch is absent), so two players doubled into the Spire see the same slot at the same instant. `elapsed` alone is seconds since THAT client's mount and would put them out of step. The ANSWER does not depend on phase, so a clock skew costs sync flavour and never solvability.
geometryChanges.cost: One extra field on the prompt. 0 draw calls.

fragmentBrief:
SIGNAL WATCH · CYCLE 21s

The five lanterns take the horizon in turn, sunwise,
four seconds each, then one second of quiet.

One lantern SPEAKS in short blinks.
Somewhere else, one lantern ANSWERS with a single long hold.

Count the blinks. They are not decoration.

Sight along a spoke of the rose to read a lantern's bearing.

REPORT: the bearing of the lantern that calls your neighbour's
lantern, then the bearing of the lantern it calls. Six digits.

(Rendered on the Fragment panel canvas. Optional diagram, and it should stay this dumb: a small compass circle with five unlabelled dots on it and one arrow between two of them, captioned "who calls whom" — it shows the SHAPE of the relation without showing a single bearing, count, or hue from the live session.)
exampleWalkthrough:
SESSION SEED rolls this configuration (verified by script):

  bearings chosen: 120, 150, 180, 240, 270   (clockwise ring order, indices 0-4)
  hues:   120 violet/Observatory · 150 gold/Spire · 180 lime/Engine
          240 vellum/Archive · 270 blue/Vault
  chain:  120 -> 240 -> 270 -> 150 -> 180 -> 120   (single 5-cycle, closes, all five visited)
  blink counts, derived as clockwise hops:
          120:3   150:1   180:3   240:1   270:2   (sum 10; not uniform, so it passes the re-roll check)

THE 21-SECOND CYCLE THE PLAYER SEES:
  t  0.0- 4.0  lantern 120 blinks 3x  ->  240 holds long
  t  4.0- 8.0  lantern 150 blinks 1x  ->  180 holds long
  t  8.0-12.0  lantern 180 blinks 3x  ->  120 holds long
  t 12.0-16.0  lantern 240 blinks 1x  ->  270 holds long
  t 16.0-20.0  lantern 270 blinks 2x  ->  150 holds long
  t 20.0-21.0  quiet, all five at resting glow
  (within a slot: blinks from +0.20s, 0.30 on / 0.30 off; pause; steady hold +2.90s to +3.90s)

PLAY, START TO FINISH:
1. The player faces south-east and catches the 240 lantern blink once, and 30 degrees round at 270 the blue window comes up and just SITS there, steady, for a full second. First click: they're answering each other.
2. They stand on the rose, face each lantern in turn, follow the gold spoke under their feet and write down five bearings: 120, 150, 180, 240, 270.
3. Over the next two cycles they collect counts: 120 blinks three, 150 blinks once, 180 blinks three, 240 blinks once, 270 blinks twice. The 180 -> 120 answer happens across almost the whole sky and they never see both ends.
4. Second click, on the pair they DID see: 240 blinked ONCE and the answer came from 270 — the very next lantern clockwise. And 270 blinked twice: count two round from 270 is 120, then 150... they check, and at t=16 the gold lantern at 150 is the one that holds. The blinks are a distance, sunwise, in lanterns.
5. They resolve the pair they could never watch: 180 blinked three — three clockwise from 180 is 240, 270, 120. So 180 calls 120. Arrows now close into one loop: 120 -> 240 -> 270 -> 150 -> 180 -> back to 120. Nowhere to start.
6. Over the call, the Archive player reads their Fragment: "RELAY LANTERN — BLUE, VAULT." The Spire player already knows which window is blue: 270.
7. Who calls 270? 240 does (its single blink). What does 270 call? 150 (its two blinks). Caller first, then callee.
8. TYPED ANSWER: 240150

WHY THE OTHER FOUR KEYS GIVE OTHER ANSWERS (same sky, same chain):
  violet/120  -> 180240      gold/150   -> 270180
  lime/180    -> 150120      vellum/240 -> 120270
Five valid-looking six-digit answers, one right, and the sky itself never says which.

SERVER CONTRACT:
  type: 'signal'
  answer: '240150'
  prompt: { kind:'signal', seed, epoch, cycleSeconds:21, instruction:'<the brief above>' }
  key:    { kind:'lantern', value:'BLUE — VAULT', label:'RELAY LANTERN' }
Derivation lives in ONE shared module (e.g. shared/spire-signal.js: deriveSpireSignal(seed) -> {bearings, hues, chain, counts}) imported by both spire.js and puzzles.js, so the room and the answer can never drift apart. Two things must change in puzzles.js: pick the builder by chamberId rather than alternating PUZZLE_TYPES by ring index, and teach wouldSolve() the 'signal' kind — recompute pred/succ for the hue the held key names and compare to the entry's own answer, or roughly one session in five hands the Spire a key that opens the Spire, which is the exact bug the file's own comment says already shipped once.
Known limit, worth stating plainly: seed + public client JS means a determined player with devtools can recompute the chain. The ANSWER never leaves the server, which is the same guarantee the cipher and sequence puzzles already give.
difficultyNotes:
WHY A 13-YEAR-OLD GETS THERE. Every atomic skill is primary-school: count up to four flashes; read a number printed on the floor; notice two lights doing the same thing; draw five arrows and see they make a loop. No astronomy, no cipher, no arithmetic beyond counting round a circle — and counting round a clock face is the one circular-counting skill every child already has. The whole thing is one sentence once you see it: "the blinks tell you how far round the answer is."

WHAT STOPS IT BEING INSTANT.
- You cannot see the sky at once. Five lanterns spread across up to 180 degrees; at a typical FOV two or three are in frame. Roughly half the caller/answerer pairs happen behind your back, so pure watching gets you a partial map and a reason to want the blink rule.
- The rule has to be induced, not read. The Fragment says the blinks matter and refuses to say how. The leap "count = number of lanterns clockwise" takes a verified example before it feels safe, and verifying costs a cycle.
- Bearings cost body movement. Sighting five lanterns down a floor spoke means walking to the rose and turning through 180 degrees, not reading a panel.
- The loop is genuinely startless. Having done everything right you hold five candidate answers and no way to choose, which is precisely when you go and talk to someone.
- Time floor: ~21s minimum to see all five speak, realistically 3-5 cycles (60-105s) of watching plus a minute of assembly. Fast crews land around 3-4 minutes; a crew that guesses eats 30s of lockout per wrong six digits.

FAILURE MODES AND THE MERCY BUILT IN.
- Miscounted blinks (3 vs 4) is the likeliest error, so the counts are capped at 4 and blinks are slow (0.6s period, ~3.3x slower than the Engine Room's 0.8Hz strobe) rather than a fast burst.
- Any count you doubt is cross-checkable against a pair you watched directly, and vice versa — two routes to one map means one bad reading is caught, not silently fatal.
- A wrong chain almost never closes into a single loop. If the arrows fork or a lantern ends up with two callers, the player knows they misread something before they ever type. Self-diagnosing, which is rare and valuable at this age.
- Colour confusion (vellum vs gold at 62m) is the one real legibility risk and is why the atlas re-tint and the 3.4 -> 4.2m quad are listed as required, not optional. The key naming both colour AND chamber is the second line of defence.

FIT FOR THE ROOM'S JOB. The Spire is where finishers wait, so the verb here is standing at a parapet watching lights on the horizon and working out who is talking to whom — a lookout's job, not a test. A finished player who wanders in has something to do immediately: hold half the sky. And a puzzle whose data is literally the other chambers signalling to each other is the only puzzle in the game that could not be moved to another room.
